cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.name: Cholesterol absorption inhibitors
cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.summary: Cholesterol absorption inhibitors are medicines that lower cholesterol by partly blocking its absorption in the small intestine. They are used on their own when a statin cannot be taken or has not worked, or alongside a statin.
cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.mechanism: Heart UK says ezetimibe partly blocks the absorption of cholesterol in the small intestine. Research reviews describe it as acting on a protein called NPC1L1 in the lining of the small intestine, which helps move cholesterol from the gut into the body. Heart UK says ezetimibe works in a different way from statins, and that the two are often combined because their effects add up.
cholesterol-absorption-inhibitors.target: Cholesterol absorption in the small intestine.
classEffects: Stomach pain, diarrhoea, extra wind and tiredness.
With a statin: muscle pain, headaches and moderately raised liver enzymes.
cautions: Unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, or yellowing of the skin or eyes, needs a doctor or NHS 111 straight away, according to the NHS.
The NHS asks people to tell their doctor about pregnancy, planning a pregnancy, breastfeeding and liver problems.
The NHS lists other cholesterol-lowering medicines such as bezafibrate and colestyramine as medicines to mention to a doctor, and UK product information advises caution with ciclosporin.

glp-1-receptor-agonists.name: GLP-1 receptor agonists
glp-1-receptor-agonists.summary: GLP-1 receptor agonists are medicines that imitate GLP-1, a hormone the body releases after eating. Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy, Rybelsus) is one; tirzepatide (Mounjaro) is described on the NHS website as acting on both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. In the UK they are used to manage type 2 diabetes and to treat obesity.
glp-1-receptor-agonists.mechanism: Semaglutide imitates GLP-1, helps people feel fuller for longer and reduces hunger, according to GOV.UK. Tirzepatide is described by the NHS as reducing appetite so that people feel fuller for longer, and it delays stomach emptying.
classEffects: Feeling sick, being sick, diarrhoea and constipation are common with semaglutide, and tirzepatide is described as commonly causing feeling sick, indigestion, constipation and diarrhoea

Pancreatitis is listed by the NHS as a rare but serious effect of semaglutide, and UK prescribing information says acute pancreatitis has been reported with tirzepatide, including necrotising and fatal cases
Severe stomach pain that does not go away needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and a 999 call if it is severe or the person is collapsing
cautions: The MHRA advises against GLP-1 receptor agonists in pregnancy because of a lack of human safety data, and advises effective contraception during treatment

The MHRA has highlighted a potential risk of stomach contents entering the lungs during general anaesthesia or deep sedation, because these medicines delay stomach emptying and food can remain despite fasting
With semaglutide, low blood sugar is more likely when it is taken with other diabetes medicines such as insulin or a sulfonylurea

classWarnings.text: The MHRA advises effective contraception during GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment because human safety data in pregnancy are limited.

mineralocorticoid-receptor-antagonists.name: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
mineralocorticoid-receptor-antagonists.summary: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, also called aldosterone antagonists, are medicines that act against the hormone aldosterone. Spironolactone and eplerenone are the two members covered here, and a Northern Care Alliance heart failure leaflet covers both.
mineralocorticoid-receptor-antagonists.mechanism: A review of spironolactone and eplerenone says they increase the amount of sodium lost in the urine and cause the kidneys to hold on to potassium when aldosterone levels are high, which is why they are described as facultative diuretics. Eplerenone is more selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor, whereas StatPearls says spironolactone also binds progesterone and androgen receptors, which underlies its anti-androgen effects such as breast enlargement in men. A 2024 meta-analysis in people with heart failure found lower rates of gynaecomastia with eplerenone than with spironolactone.
classEffects: Hyperkalaemia (high blood potassium) and acute kidney injury are described as the predominant safety concerns across the mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists in pharmacovigilance data
Gynaecomastia (breast enlargement in men) is reported more often with spironolactone than with eplerenone in a 2024 heart failure meta-analysis
cautions: US prescribing information for spironolactone says that potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, and medicines that can raise potassium, such as ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs and heparin, may lead to severe hyperkalaemia
Potassium and kidney function are checked before treatment and monitored during treatment, according to NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance for spironolactone and a review of eplerenone

sglt2-inhibitors.name: SGLT2 inhibitors
sglt2-inhibitors.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors are tablets used for type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. They lower blood sugar by acting on the kidneys, as the NHS describes for dapagliflozin.
sglt2-inhibitors.mechanism: SGLT2 stands for sodium-glucose cotransporter-2. The NHS says dapagliflozin, a medicine of this type, makes the kidneys remove extra sugar in the urine, which lowers blood sugar. Cambridge University Hospitals says the kidney and heart benefits of these medicines apply beyond people with diabetes.
classEffects: Leeds Teaching Hospitals lists genital fungal infections such as thrush as a common side effect of these medicines

Leeds Teaching Hospitals says these medicines may cause acids called ketones to build up in the blood (diabetic ketoacidosis), with warning symptoms including stomach pain, feeling sick and vomiting, rapid breathing and dehydration, which need urgent medical help (a doctor or NHS 111 promptly, or 999 in an emergency)
cautions: NHS leaflets describe sick day rules, in which the medicine is stopped temporarily during illness such as infection, diarrhoea and vomiting or flu

Severe pain, tenderness, swelling or redness around the genitals or the area between them and the anus, with fever or feeling unwell, can be a rare infection called Fournier gangrene and needs emergency help (call 999)

sulfonylureas.name: Sulfonylureas
sulfonylureas.summary: Sulfonylureas are tablets for type 2 diabetes that prompt the pancreas to make more insulin. Low blood sugar (a hypo) is one of their most common side effects, and some people gain weight. NHS diabetes guidance says to call 999 if a person with a hypo is unconscious, does not regain consciousness or has a seizure.
sulfonylureas.mechanism: Sulfonylureas work by prompting the pancreas to release more insulin, which lowers blood glucose. Diabetes UK says low blood sugar is one of the most common side effects.
classEffects: Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia), which Diabetes UK calls one of the most common side effects
Weight gain: Diabetes UK says some people gain weight while taking a sulphonylurea
Stomach upset such as tummy ache, sickness and diarrhoea
Rarer effects include liver damage and low blood cell counts, according to Diabetes UK
cautions: A hypo that leaves a person unconscious, not regaining consciousness or having a seizure is a 999 emergency, according to NHS diabetes guidance; the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if sugary food or drink does not help or hypo symptoms return
Driving: Diabetes UK says sulphonylureas can increase the risk of hypos while driving; DVLA guidance says severe hypoglycaemia while driving means stopping driving and notifying the DVLA
NICE lists a sulfonylurea among options to add when further treatment is needed in type 2 diabetes, and describes sulfonylureas as possibly increasing hypoglycaemic events and weight gain
The NHS says gliclazide is not usually used in pregnancy and lists severe kidney or liver disease among the reasons it may not be suitable

dapagliflozin.name: Dapagliflozin
dapagliflozin.summary: Dapagliflozin is a prescription tablet from the SGLT2 inhibitor group, used for type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. The NHS lists thrush, back pain and passing urine more often as common side effects. Serious effects include diabetic ketoacidosis and allergic reactions, and these need urgent medical help (a doctor or NHS 111 promptly, or 999 in an emergency).
usedFor: Type 2 diabetes, where the NHS says it is mainly used, usually when metformin cannot be taken or other medicines are not controlling blood sugar well
Heart failure, where the NHS says it can reduce the risk of the heart getting weaker and help symptoms such as tiredness
Chronic kidney disease, where the NHS says it helps to slow the rate at which the condition gets worse
NICE recommends dapagliflozin as an add-on to standard care for chronic kidney disease in adults who meet the criteria set out in its guidance (technology appraisal TA775)
NICE recommends it as an add-on to standard care for symptomatic chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction in adults (technology appraisal TA679)
NICE also recommends it for symptomatic chronic heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction (technology appraisal TA902)
dapagliflozin.howItWorks: Dapagliflozin is a type of medicine known as a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. In type 2 diabetes the NHS says it makes the kidneys remove extra sugar from the body in the urine, which lowers blood sugar. It can also reduce the amount of work the heart needs to do to pump blood around the body. In chronic kidney disease the NHS says it works by reducing pressure and swelling (inflammation) in the kidneys.
dapagliflozin.onset: The NHS says it starts to work after about 2 hours to reduce blood glucose levels, but it may take up to a week to take full effect.

common: The NHS lists thrush, back pain and passing urine more often than usual as common side effects
Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) can happen when dapagliflozin is taken with other diabetes medicines, including insulin or a sulfonylurea such as gliclazide, and can cause dizziness or shakiness
Feeling sleepy or dizzy can occur, and the NHS says driving, cycling or using tools or machines is best avoided until these symptoms pass
serious: Diabetic ketoacidosis (a build-up of acids called ketones in the blood) has symptoms such as feeling sick, unusual thirst or tiredness, stomach pain, fruity-smelling breath and faster or deeper breathing, and needs urgent medical help: a doctor or NHS 111 promptly, or 999 in an emergency
Swelling of the throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, can be a serious allergic reaction and needs an emergency 999 call

Severe pain, tenderness, swelling or redness around the genitals or the area between them and the anus, with fever or feeling unwell, can be a rare infection called Fournier gangrene and needs emergency help (call 999)

cautions: Most adults can take dapagliflozin and, for type 2 diabetes, the NHS says most children aged 10 and over can take it

The NHS says it may not be suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to it, have type 1 diabetes, have kidney or liver disease, have low blood pressure or often get urinary tract infections
Diabetes UK says treatment may need to be stopped temporarily before an operation, which the prescriber decides
The NHS advises avoiding dapagliflozin in pregnancy and breastfeeding, because there is not enough information about its effects on the baby

NHS leaflets describe sick day rules, in which dapagliflozin is stopped temporarily during illness with dehydration, such as vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or infections, and a patient leaflet says to contact the GP or NHS 111 if still unwell after 48 hours
MedlinePlus (a US source) says dapagliflozin can cause dehydration and that drinking enough water is important
Using it with insulin or a sulfonylurea raises the chance of low blood sugar, and lithium levels need closer monitoring if lithium is also taken
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk in moderation, and advises speaking to a doctor before starting a low-calorie, reduced-carbohydrate or ketogenic diet
The NHS says dapagliflozin is not stopped without talking to a doctor first, because diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease may get worse
dapagliflozin.monitoring: Lithium levels need closer monitoring in people who also take lithium. A small fall in kidney function (eGFR) can be seen when treatment starts, and further checks are decided by the prescriber.

sections.heading: What is dapagliflozin used for?
sections.body:
Dapagliflozin is a tablet that the NHS says is available only with a prescription. The NHS says it is mainly used to treat type 2 diabetes, usually when metformin cannot be taken or when the current medicine is not controlling blood sugar well. Diabetes UK says it can be taken alone or with metformin, a DPP-4 inhibitor, a sulphonylurea or insulin.

It is also used for heart failure and chronic kidney disease. In heart failure the NHS says it can reduce the risk of the heart getting weaker and help symptoms such as tiredness. In chronic kidney disease it helps to slow the rate at which the condition gets worse. NICE recommends it as an add-on to standard care for symptomatic chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction in adults, and for symptomatic chronic heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction. NICE also recommends it for chronic kidney disease in adults who meet the criteria in its guidance.

sections.heading: How does dapagliflozin work?
sections.body:
Dapagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitor, usually shortened to SGLT2 inhibitor. In type 2 diabetes the NHS says it makes the kidneys remove extra sugar in the urine, which lowers blood sugar. It can also reduce the amount of work the heart needs to do to pump blood around the body. In chronic kidney disease the NHS says it reduces pressure and swelling (inflammation) in the kidneys.

The NHS says it starts to work after about 2 hours to lower blood glucose, but it may take up to a week to take full effect. MedlinePlus says medicines of this kind help to control the condition but do not cure it.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS lists thrush, back pain and passing urine more often as common side effects. Low blood sugar can happen when it is taken with insulin or a sulfonylurea such as gliclazide, and can cause dizziness or shakiness. If a person feels sleepy or dizzy, the NHS says to avoid driving, cycling or using tools or machines until the symptoms pass.

Serious effects include diabetic ketoacidosis, in which acids called ketones build up in the blood, according to Leeds Teaching Hospitals. Symptoms include feeling sick, unusual thirst or tiredness, stomach pain, fruity-smelling breath and faster or deeper breathing. The NHS says these symptoms usually develop over 24 hours but can come on faster, and they need urgent medical help: a doctor or NHS 111 promptly, or 999 in an emergency. Swelling of the throat or tongue, or difficulty breathing, can be a serious allergic reaction and needs a 999 call. Severe pain, tenderness, swelling or redness around the genitals or the area between them and the anus, with fever or feeling unwell, can be a rare infection called Fournier gangrene and needs emergency help (call 999).

sections.heading: Illness, alcohol and food
sections.body:
NHS leaflets describe sick day rules, in which dapagliflozin is stopped temporarily during illness with dehydration, such as vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or infections. A patient leaflet says to contact the GP or NHS 111 if still unwell after 48 hours. MedlinePlus, a US source, says the medicine can cause dehydration and that drinking enough water is important.

The NHS says people can eat and drink normally, and that alcohol can be drunk in moderation. It suggests speaking to a doctor before starting a low-calorie, reduced-carbohydrate or ketogenic diet. The NHS says the medicine itself does not affect the ability to drive, but low blood sugar can, which is possible when it is taken with insulin or a sulfonylurea.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care?
sections.body:
Most adults can take dapagliflozin, and the NHS says most children aged 10 and over can take it for type 2 diabetes. It may not be suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to it, have type 1 diabetes, have kidney or liver disease, have low blood pressure or often get urinary tract infections. The NHS advises avoiding it in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and Diabetes UK says treatment may need to be stopped temporarily before an operation.

Lithium levels need closer monitoring if both medicines are taken. The NHS says dapagliflozin is not stopped without talking to a doctor first, because diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease may get worse.

faqs.q: Is dapagliflozin only for diabetes?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says it is mainly used for type 2 diabetes but is also used for heart failure and chronic kidney disease. In heart failure it can reduce the risk of the heart getting weaker, and in kidney disease it helps to slow the rate at which the condition gets worse.

faqs.q: How long is dapagliflozin taken for?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is usually needed long term. It is not stopped without talking to a doctor first, because diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease may get worse.

faqs.q: What are sick day rules?
faqs.a: They are advice to stop dapagliflozin temporarily during illness with dehydration, such as vomiting, diarrhoea or fever. A patient leaflet says to contact the GP or NHS 111 if still unwell after 48 hours.

faqs.q: Does dapagliflozin cause thrush?
faqs.a: The NHS lists thrush as a common side effect. Leeds Teaching Hospitals also lists genital fungal infections such as thrush as a common side effect of SGLT2 inhibitors.

empagliflozin.name: Empagliflozin
empagliflozin.summary: Empagliflozin is a prescription medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. It is a sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor, and its brand name is Jardiance. The main cautions include thrush, dehydration when it is combined with diuretics, and a serious build-up of ketones called diabetic ketoacidosis, which the NHS says needs a 999 call if suspected.
usedFor: Type 2 diabetes, to lower blood sugar levels
Heart failure, including symptomatic chronic heart failure as recommended by NICE
Chronic kidney disease in adults, as recommended by NICE under specific conditions
empagliflozin.howItWorks: Empagliflozin is a type of medicine known as a sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. In diabetes it lowers blood sugar by helping remove extra sugar from the body through the urine. In heart failure it reduces the amount of work the heart has to do.
empagliflozin.onset: The NHS says it starts to lower blood sugar after about 1 to 2 hours and may take up to a week to work fully, while in heart failure it can be a month or 2 before symptoms improve.

common: The NHS lists thrush, needing to pee more often, feeling more thirsty than usual and skin rash as common side effects.
The NHS says low blood sugar can happen if meals are skipped, alcohol is drunk or other diabetes medicines are taken.
serious: Diabetic ketoacidosis can make a person feel very thirsty, confused or unusually tired, or give breath that smells sweet, and the NHS says to call 999 if it is suspected; Diabetes UK describes it as a rare side effect.

Fournier's gangrene is a rare but serious genital infection that can cause severe pain, tenderness, redness or swelling in the genital area with a high temperature or feeling unwell; the NHS says to call 999 if it is suspected, and its side-effects page says to tell a doctor or call 111 straight away.
A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), with swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, needs a 999 call.
The NHS says to call 111 straight away for signs of dehydration.

cautions: The NHS says most adults can take it, and suggests checking with a doctor for people aged 75 or older.
It is not used to treat type 1 diabetes.
The NHS lists a past allergic reaction, low blood pressure, severe kidney or liver disease, frequent urinary tract infections and upcoming surgery as reasons to check with a doctor first.

NHS information lists diuretics (water tablets) and blood pressure medicines among medicines that interact with it, and the UK product information says it may add to the diuretic effect of thiazide and loop diuretics and may increase the risk of dehydration and low blood pressure.

The NHS says it is not recommended in pregnancy because there is little information about whether it could affect the baby, and not usually recommended while breastfeeding because it is not known how much passes into breast milk.
The NHS says the tablets may need to be stopped before an operation if eating has to stop, and during recovery, because of the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with it, but alcohol can increase the risk of low blood sugar and of side effects such as diabetic ketoacidosis, so it advises trying to limit how much is drunk.
An NHS hospital trust leaflet says that passing more glucose in the urine increases the risk of a urinary tract infection.
empagliflozin.monitoring: For chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, NICE says a heart failure specialist should advise on starting empagliflozin and monitoring should be done by the most appropriate healthcare professional.

sections.heading: What is empagliflozin used for?
sections.body: Empagliflozin is used to treat type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Its brand name is Jardiance, and it is not used for type 1 diabetes. It comes as tablets, and the NHS says it is only available with a prescription. For heart failure, NICE recommends it as an option for symptomatic chronic heart failure, both with reduced ejection fraction and with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction. NICE says treatment should start on the advice of a heart failure specialist. Where several options are suitable, including dapagliflozin, NICE guidance on preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction says the least expensive should be used. For chronic kidney disease, NICE recommends it for adults only under specific conditions, including as an add-on to optimised standard care with the highest tolerated licensed dose of an ACE inhibitor or ARB, unless those are contraindicated. The NHS says treatment for diabetes, heart failure or chronic kidney disease is usually for life.

sections.heading: How does empagliflozin work and how soon?
sections.body: Empagliflozin is a sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. In diabetes it helps remove extra sugar from the body through the urine, so blood sugar falls. In heart failure it reduces the work the heart has to do. The NHS says it starts to work after about 1 to 2 hours to lower blood sugar, but it may take up to a week to work fully. In heart failure it might be a month or 2 before symptoms improve, and the NHS says it is still reducing the heart's workload even if no change is noticed. The NHS says it does not make people put on weight, and some people lose weight. The NHS advises against stopping it without talking to a doctor first.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of empagliflozin?
sections.body: The NHS lists thrush, needing to pee more often, feeling thirstier than usual and skin rash as the common side effects. The NHS says a pharmacist can recommend an antifungal treatment for thrush. The NHS says low blood sugar can happen if meals are skipped, alcohol is drunk or other diabetes medicines are taken. The NHS describes more serious side effects as rare. Diabetic ketoacidosis, where ketones build up in the body, can cause great thirst, confusion, unusual tiredness or sweet-smelling breath, and the NHS lists feeling or being sick, stomach pain and deeper or faster breathing among other signs. The NHS says to call 999 if diabetic ketoacidosis, anaphylaxis or Fournier's gangrene is suspected. Fournier's gangrene, a serious genital infection, can cause severe pain, tenderness, redness or swelling in the genital area with a high temperature or feeling unwell, and the NHS side-effects page says to tell a doctor or call 111 straight away. Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or struggling to breathe, may be anaphylaxis and needs a 999 call. The NHS says to call 111 straight away for signs of dehydration.

sections.heading: Taking empagliflozin with other medicines, alcohol and during illness
sections.body: NHS information lists diuretics and medicines that lower blood pressure among medicines that interact with empagliflozin. The UK product information says it may add to the diuretic effect of thiazide and loop diuretics and may increase the risk of dehydration and low blood pressure. The NHS says people can drink alcohol while taking empagliflozin, but alcohol can increase the risk of low blood sugar levels. It advises trying to limit how much alcohol is drunk, because alcohol can increase the risk of side effects such as diabetic ketoacidosis. The NHS says the tablets may need to be stopped before an operation if eating has to stop, and while recovering afterwards, because of the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis. An NHS hospital trust leaflet says that passing more glucose in the urine increases the risk of a urinary tract infection.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with empagliflozin?
sections.body: The NHS says most adults can take empagliflozin and suggests checking with a doctor for people aged 75 or older. It also lists a past allergic reaction, low blood pressure, severe kidney or liver disease, frequent urinary tract infections and upcoming surgery as reasons for a doctor to check first. The NHS says it is not suitable for people with type 1 diabetes or at higher risk of diabetic ketoacidosis. The NHS says it is not recommended in pregnancy because there is little information about whether it could affect the baby. For breastfeeding, the NHS says it is not usually recommended because it is not known how much passes into breast milk, and a doctor may suggest an alternative.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking empagliflozin?
faqs.a: The NHS says people can drink alcohol while taking empagliflozin. However, alcohol can increase the risk of low blood sugar levels. The NHS advises trying to limit how much alcohol is drunk, because it can increase the risk of side effects such as diabetic ketoacidosis.

faqs.q: How long does empagliflozin take to work?
faqs.a: The NHS says it starts to lower blood sugar after about 1 to 2 hours, though it may take up to a week to work fully. In heart failure it might be a month or 2 before symptoms improve. The NHS says it is still reducing the heart's workload even if no change is noticed.

faqs.q: Does empagliflozin cause weight gain?
faqs.a: The NHS says empagliflozin does not make people put on weight. Some people find they lose weight.

faqs.q: Is empagliflozin used in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says empagliflozin is not recommended in pregnancy because there is little information about whether it could affect the baby. For breastfeeding, the NHS says it is not usually recommended because it is not known how much passes into breast milk. The NHS says that if someone is pregnant or planning a pregnancy, the doctor may switch them to another medicine.

faqs.q: What are the signs of a serious side effect?
faqs.a: Diabetic ketoacidosis can cause great thirst, confusion, unusual tiredness or sweet-smelling breath, and the NHS says to call 999 if it is suspected. Severe pain, tenderness, redness or swelling in the genital area with a high temperature or feeling unwell may be Fournier's gangrene, and the NHS says to call 999 if it is suspected. Sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue needs a 999 call.

sections.heading: What is gliclazide used for?
sections.body: Gliclazide is a medicine for type 2 diabetes that belongs to a group called sulfonylureas. In type 2 diabetes the body does not make or use insulin well enough, so sugar builds up in the blood. Diabetes UK says gliclazide comes as standard-release or slow-release tablets. Diabetes UK describes gliclazide as one of four sulphonylureas that people with type 2 diabetes in the UK can be prescribed. The NHS says most adults and children aged 12 years and over can take it, but it is not suitable for everyone. The NHS lists type 1 diabetes, a past allergic reaction, diabetic ketoacidosis, severe kidney or liver disease, porphyria and G6PD deficiency among the reasons it may not be suitable.

sections.heading: How does gliclazide work?
sections.body: Gliclazide works by prompting the pancreas to make more insulin. Insulin is a hormone made in the pancreas that helps move sugar from the blood into the body's cells. A UK formulary guide says gliclazide directly stimulates insulin release, so it has the potential to cause hypoglycaemia.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of gliclazide?
sections.body: Diabetes UK lists tummy ache, sickness and diarrhoea among the common effects of sulphonylureas. The NHS says side effects can be less likely if the tablets are taken with a meal. Diabetes UK says some people gain weight while taking a sulphonylurea. Diabetes UK says rarer effects of sulphonylureas include liver damage and low blood cell counts. The NHS lists three rarer, serious problems: an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), a problem with the blood cells and problems with the liver. Warning signs of a blood cell problem include paleness, unusual bleeding or bruising, a sore throat and fever, and a liver problem can turn the skin or the whites of the eyes yellow. The NHS says to call 999 for a suspected anaphylaxis, with signs such as a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing. For other suspected serious side effects the NHS says to call NHS 111.

sections.heading: Low blood sugar, driving and alcohol
sections.body: Low blood sugar, called hypoglycaemia or a hypo, is a common side effect of gliclazide. The NHS says it can cause dizziness, feeling sick, being very hungry or being very tired. Diabetes UK says hypos are more likely when a meal is missed, after strenuous exercise or after drinking alcohol. The usual response the NHS describes is to eat or drink something sugary to raise blood sugar quickly. The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if the sugary food or drink does not help or the symptoms return. If a person with a hypo becomes unconscious, does not begin to regain consciousness, or shows signs of a seizure, NHS diabetes guidance says to call 999 straight away. NHS hospital guidance says nothing is given by mouth to someone who is unconscious or fitting, because of the risk of choking. The NHS says a person who has taken more than the prescribed amount of gliclazide should call NHS 111. The NHS says that if gliclazide makes a person feel sleepy or dizzy, they should not drive until the symptoms pass. Diabetes UK says sulphonylureas can increase the risk of hypos while driving. DVLA guidance says a driver who has an episode of severe hypoglycaemia while driving must stop driving and tell the DVLA, and it defines severe as needing another person's help. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with gliclazide but more alcohol can raise the risk of low blood sugar, while UK manufacturer leaflets say drinking alcohol is not recommended because it can alter diabetes control.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what is checked?
sections.body: The NHS says gliclazide is not usually used in pregnancy, and a doctor may offer a different medicine. The NHS also advises against it during breastfeeding. The NHS says some antibiotics and antifungals, steroid tablets, NSAID painkillers and other diabetes medicines can cause low blood sugar when taken with gliclazide. The NHS says ibuprofen and aspirin should be checked with a pharmacist or doctor first, because they can lower blood sugar too much. The NHS says St John's wort should not be taken, because it may change how the body processes gliclazide. The NHS advises checking with a pharmacist or doctor before combining gliclazide with any medicine, herbal remedy, vitamin or supplement. UK prescribing information lists miconazole, an antifungal, as a contraindicated combination because it increases the blood-sugar-lowering effect. The NHS says to tell the doctor before an operation, because gliclazide increases the risk of low blood sugar during surgery. A UK formulary guide says HbA1c shows overall diabetes control but cannot show day-to-day swings in blood glucose or hypoglycaemia. NICE advises considering short-term self-monitoring of blood glucose in adults with type 2 diabetes when starting corticosteroids or to confirm suspected hypoglycaemia. NICE sets a different HbA1c aim for adults taking a drug associated with hypoglycaemia.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk with gliclazide?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk with gliclazide, but more alcohol can raise the risk of low blood sugar. UK manufacturer leaflets say drinking alcohol is not recommended because it can alter diabetes control.

faqs.q: What happens if blood sugar drops too low?
faqs.a: Low blood sugar is called a hypo, and the NHS says the usual response is to eat or drink something sugary. The NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 if sugary food or drink does not help or the symptoms return. If the person becomes unconscious, does not begin to regain consciousness, or has signs of a seizure, NHS diabetes guidance says to call 999 straight away.

faqs.q: Can gliclazide be used in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says gliclazide is not usually used in pregnancy, and a doctor may offer a different medicine. The NHS also advises against it during breastfeeding.

faqs.q: Does gliclazide affect driving?
faqs.a: The NHS says that if gliclazide makes a person feel sleepy or dizzy, they should not drive until the symptoms pass. The DVLA says a driver who has an episode of severe hypoglycaemia while driving must stop driving and tell the DVLA.

sections.heading: What is semaglutide used for?
sections.body:
Semaglutide is a prescription medicine. The NHS says it is used to manage type 2 diabetes (Ozempic and Rybelsus) or to treat obesity (Wegovy). Ozempic and Wegovy are injections in pre-filled pens, and Rybelsus is a tablet. Diabetes UK says Ozempic should only be prescribed to people with type 2 diabetes. The NHS says that for weight loss it is used together with exercise and changes to diet.

For weight management, NICE recommends Wegovy for adults only within a specialist multidisciplinary weight management service, for a maximum of two years. Diabetes UK says NICE recommends it for adults with a high body mass index (BMI) and at least one weight-related condition, and for some adults with a lower BMI who meet criteria for referral to specialist services. Diabetes UK also notes that access to specialist weight management services varies. Diabetes UK says Wegovy might be prescribed to adults with cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight to lower the risk of major events such as heart attack or stroke.

sections.heading: How does semaglutide work?
sections.body: Semaglutide belongs to the GLP-1 receptor agonist group of medicines. It imitates GLP-1, a hormone the body releases after eating. It helps people feel fuller for longer and reduces hunger. It also increases the insulin the pancreas releases in response to food, according to an NHS hospital leaflet on the tablet form. Like other GLP-1 medicines, it delays emptying of the stomach, according to the MHRA. Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) is described on the NHS website as acting on both GIP and GLP-1 receptors, so it is related but not identical.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of semaglutide?
sections.body:
The NHS lists feeling sick, being sick, diarrhoea and constipation as common side effects. Feeling tired, reactions where the injection goes in, and hair loss are also listed. The US Ozempic label notes that nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea are most common when treatment is first started.

Inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis) is rare but serious. Its sign is severe pain in the stomach or back that does not go away. That pain needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and a 999 call if it is severe or the person is collapsing. Diabetes UK says a sudden change in eyesight, such as sudden loss of vision, needs urgent medical advice. In February 2026 the MHRA updated its guidance on semaglutide and NAION, a very rare eye condition that typically causes sudden, painless vision loss in one eye. A severe allergic reaction is also listed by the NHS as a serious effect.

Gallstones were reported more often with semaglutide than with comparison treatments in clinical studies, according to the UK summary of product characteristics. That document also says vomiting and diarrhoea can cause dehydration, which in rare cases can lead to worse kidney function, so care to avoid losing fluid is advised.

sections.heading: Taking semaglutide with other medicines, alcohol and in pregnancy
sections.body:
The NHS says low blood sugar is more likely when semaglutide is taken with other diabetes medicines such as insulin or a sulfonylurea. Symptoms include sweating, shaking, a fast heartbeat and dizziness. The UK summary of product characteristics says a lower dose of insulin or a sulfonylurea should be considered when semaglutide is added. The NHS says drinking alcohol can increase side effects such as feeling or being sick.

The NHS says semaglutide should not be used in pregnancy, and advises stopping it before trying to become pregnant. The MHRA advises against GLP-1 receptor agonists in pregnancy and advises effective contraception throughout treatment, because human safety data are lacking. Diabetes UK says semaglutide should not be used while breastfeeding.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and what happens when treatment stops?
sections.body:
In a large heart-outcomes study, diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye condition, was reported more often with semaglutide than placebo, mainly in people using insulin who already had it. Rapid improvement in blood glucose control has been linked to a temporary worsening of retinopathy, and people with the condition are monitored closely, according to the UK summary of product characteristics. The NHS lists having or having had an inflamed pancreas among the reasons semaglutide may not be suitable.

The MHRA has highlighted a potential risk of stomach contents entering the lungs during general anaesthesia or deep sedation. This is because GLP-1 medicines delay the emptying of the stomach, so food can remain there despite fasting.

NICE includes a rule for stopping Wegovy if early weight loss is too small. NICE says many people regain weight after stopping obesity treatment if they do not get the right support.

faqs.q: Is Ozempic the same as Wegovy?
faqs.a: Both contain semaglutide. The NHS lists Ozempic and Rybelsus for managing type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for treating obesity. Diabetes UK says Ozempic should only be prescribed to people with type 2 diabetes. NICE recommends Wegovy for weight management within a specialist weight management service.

faqs.q: Can semaglutide cause pancreatitis?
faqs.a: Pancreatitis, inflammation of the pancreas, is a rare but serious side effect listed by the NHS. The sign is severe pain in the stomach or back that does not go away. That needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and a 999 call if the pain is severe or the person is collapsing.

faqs.q: Can semaglutide be used in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says semaglutide should not be used in pregnancy. The MHRA advises effective contraception throughout treatment with GLP-1 receptor agonists, and the NHS advises stopping semaglutide before trying to become pregnant.

sections.heading: What is spironolactone used for?
sections.body:
Spironolactone is a diuretic, a medicine that helps reduce fluid build-up in the body. UK product information lists oedema (fluid swelling) linked to heart failure, to cirrhosis of the liver with ascites, to malignant ascites and to nephrotic syndrome. An older-format Aldactone product summary on emc also lists primary hyperaldosteronism, both for diagnosis and for treatment.

The British Association of Dermatologists says spironolactone is used off licence for women with acne, which means it is not specifically indicated for that use in the UK prescribing licence, although it is still usually available on the NHS. A Gloucestershire hospital leaflet says it does not cure acne but can help manage and even clear it over time. In the UK it is sold under brand names including Aldactone tablets, Qaialdo oral suspension and Urospir oral solution. The Urospir product information says switching between the solution and other spironolactone products should be avoided if possible.

sections.heading: How does spironolactone work?
sections.body: Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist, which means it acts against the hormone aldosterone. A review of spironolactone and eplerenone says they increase the amount of sodium lost in the urine and cause the kidneys to hold on to potassium when aldosterone levels are high. Because it keeps potassium in the body, spironolactone belongs to the group known as potassium-sparing diuretics. Eplerenone is a related medicine that is more selective for the aldosterone receptor, while StatPearls says spironolactone also binds progesterone and androgen receptors, which underlies its anti-androgen effects such as breast enlargement in men. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis in people with heart failure found lower rates of gynaecomastia with eplerenone than with spironolactone.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of spironolactone?
sections.body:
Dizziness, feeling sick (nausea), muscle or leg cramps and tiredness are among the common side effects the NHS lists. The NHS also lists breast pain or breast enlargement, including in men, as a common side effect. The Aldactone patient leaflet lists menstrual problems in women as uncommon, and breast pain as common in men and uncommon in women. A Northern Care Alliance heart failure leaflet describes breast swelling or tenderness, especially in men, as a rare effect, so the stated frequency differs between sources.

Spironolactone can raise potassium levels in the blood (hyperkalaemia), which can cause muscle weakness, tiredness, numbness and an irregular heartbeat. A hospital leaflet for acne use lists high blood potassium as very rare and more likely in people over 45 or with heart or kidney problems. Spironolactone can sometimes affect kidney function as well as raising potassium.

The NHS lists a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) as a possible side effect, with symptoms including a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash and difficulty breathing. Symptoms that could point to high potassium need prompt advice from NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and a possible serious allergic reaction is an emergency needing a 999 call. Yellow skin or eyes (jaundice) are listed in UK patient leaflets, which say spironolactone can impair liver function and that a doctor should be told straight away.

sections.heading: Taking spironolactone with other medicines, food and salt substitutes
sections.body: The US prescribing information says that potassium supplements, potassium-containing salt substitutes, a potassium-rich diet, or medicines that can raise potassium, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II antagonists, NSAIDs, heparin and low molecular weight heparin, may lead to severe hyperkalaemia. The UK product summary lists use with eplerenone or other potassium-sparing diuretics as a contraindication. The same US label says NSAIDs may reduce the diuretic, natriuretic and antihypertensive effect of spironolactone. An NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service monitoring guide gives patient advice to avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers unless prescribed and to avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes. The NHS page says eating high-potassium foods such as bananas and avocados, or using salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt, can raise potassium levels further. The MHRA has published a Drug Safety Update on the risk of potentially fatal hyperkalaemia when spironolactone is used with renin-angiotensin system drugs in heart failure.

sections.body:
The NHS says it may not suit people with severe kidney problems or a history of high blood potassium, and hospital leaflets also list Addison's disease. The NHS says spironolactone is not usually recommended in pregnancy, and a hospital leaflet advises against it in anyone pregnant or trying to conceive. The NHS says breastfeeding may be possible but should be checked with a doctor or healthcare professional first. sections.heading: What is tirzepatide used for?
sections.body:
Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine used to manage type 2 diabetes and to treat obesity. In the UK it is sold under the brand name Mounjaro. It is an injection that people give themselves.

NICE has recommended tirzepatide for some adults with type 2 diabetes who meet set criteria, alongside diet and exercise. NICE has also recommended it as an option for adults with overweight or obesity, alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. NICE links this to a person's starting body mass index and to having at least one weight-related health condition. NICE applies a lower body mass index threshold for people from some ethnic backgrounds.

For weight management, the NHS says tirzepatide is only prescribed alongside programmes that support changes to diet and physical activity.

sections.heading: How does tirzepatide work?
sections.body:
Tirzepatide activates the receptors for two gut hormones, GLP-1 and GIP, so it is called a dual agonist. For weight loss, the NHS says it reduces appetite and helps people feel fuller for longer. For type 2 diabetes, it lowers blood sugar and helps the body make more insulin when needed. An NHS medicines optimisation newsletter adds that it increases insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon release and slows the emptying of the stomach.

NICE says it can be used in primary care or in specialist weight management services. Access on the NHS in England is being phased in, so not everyone who fits the NICE recommendation can have it at once. NHS England's interim commissioning guidance sets out which groups are offered it first.

sections.heading: What side effects can tirzepatide cause?
sections.body:
The NHS lists feeling sick and being sick among the common side effects. It also lists constipation, diarrhoea, stomach pain, tiredness, hair loss and redness at the injection site. The NHS says most serious side effects are rare.

The NHS lists inflammation of the pancreas (acute pancreatitis), which can cause severe pain in the stomach or back that does not go away, as a serious side effect. The NHS also lists gallstones or swelling of the gallbladder, which can cause severe tummy pain. A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) can cause a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing. Severe pain that does not go away needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or the GP, and signs of a serious allergic reaction are an emergency that needs a 999 call.

The NHS lists low blood sugar, which is more likely when tirzepatide is used with other diabetes medicines and can cause headaches, vision problems, feeling dizzy, weak or confused, a fast heartbeat or sweating. A South West London NHS information sheet for prescribers warns that sickness and diarrhoea can lead to dehydration, which could worsen kidney function.

sections.heading: Tirzepatide with contraception, alcohol and other medicines
sections.body:
The MHRA says GLP-1 medicines may reduce how well oral contraceptives work in people who are overweight or obese. For people who are overweight and taking Mounjaro, the MHRA advises using a non-oral method of contraception in addition to the pill. The MHRA lists the pill and non-oral methods such as the implant, coil or condoms as effective contraception.

The NHS says it is best to avoid alcohol, because alcohol can increase side effects such as feeling or being sick. Low blood sugar is more likely when tirzepatide is combined with other diabetes medicines.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with tirzepatide?
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults can use tirzepatide. It may not suit people who have had an allergic reaction to tirzepatide or a similar GLP-1 medicine, or who have had acute pancreatitis.

The NHS says tirzepatide is not used in pregnancy because there is not enough information about its effects on a baby. The MHRA says GLP-1 medicines should not be taken during pregnancy, while trying to get pregnant or during breastfeeding, because of a lack of human data. The MHRA also advises that people who could become pregnant take steps to avoid pregnancy while using GLP-1 medicines. The NHS says it is not known whether tirzepatide passes into breast milk.

NICE says that if too little of the starting weight has been lost after six months at the highest tolerated dose, the prescriber decides whether to continue, weighing the benefits and risks for that person.

faqs.a: In the UK it is sold under the brand name Mounjaro. Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine used to manage type 2 diabetes and to treat obesity. It is an injection that people give themselves. The NHS says it is available only with a prescription, either on the NHS or privately.

faqs.a: The MHRA says GLP-1 medicines may reduce how well oral contraceptives work in people who are overweight or obese. For people who are overweight and taking Mounjaro, the MHRA advises using a non-oral method of contraception in addition to the pill.
